clinicalPearls: A recognisable syndrome combining macrodontia of the upper central incisors with a characteristic face and developmental delay
Large upper central incisors (macrodontia) are a near-specific clue and give the syndrome its dental signature
Facial features include a triangular face, a broad eyebrow with a tendency to meet in the midline (synophrys), a prominent nasal bridge and a long philtrum
Short stature, delayed bone age, skeletal and hand anomalies (such as brachydactyly and clinodactyly) are common
Developmental delay is usually mild to moderate, with behavioural difficulties, autistic features, hearing loss and epilepsy in some
Caused by loss-of-function variants in ANKRD11 (or 16q24.3 deletions including it), usually autosomal dominant, encoding a chromatin regulator that interacts with histone deacetylase complexes
The name derives from the initials of the surnames in the original family descriptions
reference.pathophysiology: ANKRD11 encodes ankyrin repeat domain 11, a chromatin regulator that interacts with histone deacetylase complexes to modulate histone acetylation and thereby the transcription of genes controlling neural development and bone formation. Loss-of-function variants or deletions cause haploinsufficiency, dysregulating chromatin-dependent gene expression during development of the brain, skeleton and teeth. This produces the intellectual disability, characteristic facies, macrodontia and skeletal features. As a chromatin-modifying regulator, it belongs to the broad group of disorders in which altered histone regulation disturbs neurodevelopment.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated short stature with delayed bone age
additionalInvestigations: Dental assessment noting macrodontia of the upper central incisors
Bone-age radiograph, skeletal survey and growth assessment
EEG and brain MRI where seizures or other neurological features occur
Chromosomal microarray for 16q24.3 deletions and gene panel or exome sequencing including ANKRD11
redFlags: Feeding difficulty or faltering growth in infancy
Cardiac or other structural anomalies needing evaluation
reference.prognosis: KBG syndrome generally has a favourable outlook, with mild to moderate intellectual disability and manageable skeletal, dental and sensory features; most individuals achieve meaningful independence with support. Care is supportive with dental, audiological and developmental surveillance.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis when macrodontia is subtle or the child is pre-dentate
Confusing it with Cornelia de Lange syndrome based on synophrys alone
Overlooking hearing loss that affects speech and learning
Relying only on sequencing and missing 16q24.3 deletions detectable by microarray
management: Early developmental intervention with speech, occupational and physiotherapy for the developmental delay
Dental review and orthodontic management of macrodontia and malocclusion of the upper central incisors
Audiological surveillance with hearing aids for conductive or sensorineural hearing loss
Growth and skeletal monitoring with bone-age assessment, and endocrine referral to consider growth hormone evaluation where short stature warrants
Antiseizure medication and neurology input for those who develop epilepsy
Behavioural and educational support addressing autistic features, attention difficulties and learning needs
Clinical genetics referral with counselling for this autosomal dominant ANKRD11 disorder and testing of at-risk relatives
